title: Maize import restrictions put Sri Lanka’s poultry export ambitions at risk | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 20 October 2026 05:25
-     - 10

Sri Lanka’s poultry industry faces a policy contradiction. The Government restricts maize imports to protect domestic growers while seeking to increase chicken and egg production and develop poultry exports. Yet maize is a principal feed ingredient, and uncertainty over its availability and price raises costs throughout the industry.

The question is not whether maize farmers deserve protection. It is whether that protection can be delivered without constraining feed manufacturers, poultry producers, consumers and exporters. A sustainable policy must reconcile agricultural incomes with food affordability, livestock production and export competitiveness.

A persistent gap in maize supply

Government estimates published in 2022 placed annual maize requirements for animal feed at about 700,000 metric tons. This benchmark needs updating as poultry production expands, but it illustrates the scale of demand.

According to the Department of Animal Production and Health (DAPH), domestic maize output in the two cultivation seasons of 2024 totalled 223,497 metric tons, less than one-third of that estimated feed requirement. DAPH recorded 221,935 metric tons of maize imported for animal feed during the year. World Bank World Integrated Trade Solution (WITS) figures put overall non-seed maize imports at 251,843 tons. The figures cover different import categories and should not be treated as interchangeable.

Moreover, domestic maize also supplies Thriposha production and human consumption. Not all locally grown maize is available to poultry producers. The Food and Agriculture Organization estimated production at approximately 420,000 tons in 2025, suggesting a recovery in output, but not the elimination of seasonal supply risks.

These figures highlight the need for a current, disaggregated assessment of maize demand, domestic harvests and stocks. The 700,000-tonne estimate relates to feed requirements, while production and import figures cover different years and uses. A simple subtraction cannot establish the exact shortage. Authorities need to account for carry-over stocks, alternative feed ingredients and the timing of harvests and imports. Without that evidence, import decisions risk being disconnected from actual requirements and seasonal availability.

Farmer protection and its cost

The case for protecting maize growers is legitimate. Large imports during harvesting periods could depress farm-gate prices, particularly for smallholders lacking drying, storage and pre-agreed purchasing arrangements. However, restrictions imposed when local maize is insufficient can create scarcity and push up prices for feed manufacturers.

DAPH attributed inflationary maize prices in 2024 partly to restricted import periods and controlled volumes. The domestic maize price rose from roughly Rs. 130 per kilogram in January to Rs. 191 by November. Farmers able to sell at higher prices may benefit, but poultry producers face increased input costs.

In March 2026, the Cabinet approved a mechanism for registered feed manufacturers and importers to bring in maize to cover shortages outside harvesting periods. Subsequent restrictions linked to pressure on the rupee nevertheless renewed uncertainty. An import framework cannot support production planning if quantities and approvals change without clear supply data or advance notice.

Uncertain quotas can also favour firms with privileged access to permits, rather than the most efficient feed manufacturers. Farmers need assured buyers and fair harvest prices; the downstream industry needs sufficient raw materials. Better market information and competitive procurement would help reconcile both interests.

How maize taxation reaches the poultry farm

The Special Commodity Levy on imported maize increased from Rs. 25 to Rs. 50 per kilogram in May 2026. That is an additional Rs. 25,000 per imported metric tonne, before considering how costs are shared along the supply chain.

The effect on feed can be illustrated simply. If maize accounts for 50% of a feed formulation and the full Rs. 25 per kilogram increase is passed through, the additional input cost could reach Rs. 12.50 per kilogram of feed. This is an illustration, not an observed retail price increase: the result depends on the mix of local and imported maize, inventories, feed recipes and pricing decisions.

The 2026 tariff framework cited in the original analysis also lists customs duty, VAT, Cess and the Social Security Contribution Levy. Their applicability, interaction with the Special Commodity Levy and any exemptions require checking before calculating an effective import-tax burden.

The economic issue remains clear: costly or delayed maize imports raise the risk of more expensive poultry feed. That cost is not confined to large processors. Independent feed mills and small poultry farms may have limited bargaining power and fewer options to change suppliers, making them more exposed to sudden price increases. Import taxes should be evaluated alongside domestic output and feed-price data, not in isolation.

Higher output does not guarantee profitability

Feed is among the largest expenses in broiler and layer production. Higher feed prices raise the cost of chicken meat and eggs, but producers cannot necessarily pass increases to consumers, especially when growing supplies put downward pressure on selling prices.

DAPH figures show poultry meat production rising from approximately 236,110 tons in 2023 to 258,540 tons in 2024. Egg output increased from 2,043.5 million to 2,953.06 million over the same period. These gains show the industry’s productive capacity, but they do not establish that farmers earned better margins.

Smaller farms are especially exposed. They have less capacity to purchase inputs in bulk, hold inventories or absorb price swings. When selling prices ease while feed costs remain high, investment and future production become harder to sustain. This matters for household access to affordable animal protein as well as for the industry’s growth.

A wider test of fiscal policy

Maize import taxes generate revenue and support domestic producer prices, but those benefits have an economic cost. Expensive feed can discourage investment in farms, feed mills, processing plants, cold storage and higher-value products. It can also limit employment, future export earnings and taxable profits generated elsewhere in the value chain.

The policy test should therefore extend beyond customs collections. Government must assess the combined effects on maize growers, poultry farmers, consumers, investors and public revenue.

A tariff that raises revenue at the border may still reduce the potential economic return from poultry production. Exchange-rate concerns deserve consideration because imports require foreign currency. Yet a longer-term assessment should also account for foreign exchange earned from poultry exports and the possibility that more efficient production could replace costly finished-food imports.

The appropriate test is the net economic benefit, not the maize import bill alone.

Exports are growing, but from a modest base

Sri Lanka already exports poultry products. DAPH reported exports of approximately 1,576 tons in 2024, increasing to nearly 2,610 tons in 2025, with a reported value of about Rs. 1.06 billion. The growth is encouraging, although export volumes remain small relative to domestic production.

The Maldives and selected markets in the Middle East and Asia offer possible opportunities for frozen, processed and value-added poultry products. However, access depends on competitive prices, reliable supply, animal-disease management, traceability, food-safety certification and cold-chain logistics.

Feed costs are central to this calculation. Sri Lankan processors cannot build lasting export relationships if maize is intermittently unavailable or disproportionately expensive compared with competitors’ inputs. Likewise, stronger processing capacity alone cannot offset an unpredictable raw-material policy.

DAPH’s 2025 poultry industry analysis identified maize import rules, taxation and approval procedures as areas requiring review.

Export growth will also depend on sustained production volumes and consistent product specifications. Buyers are unlikely to commit to long-term contracts when processors cannot reliably estimate input costs.

The competitiveness issue therefore runs from maize procurement through farming and processing to refrigerated shipment. Input-policy reform is necessary, although it will not be sufficient on its own.

Industry seeks predictable supplies

Sri Lanka Poultry Producers’ Industry Association President Dr. Ajith Gunawardena has raised concerns over the disruption caused by maize import restrictions.

According to Gunawardena, permission had been given to import approximately 300,000 tons, but imports were subsequently curtailed amid pressure on the rupee. Companies that had already opened letters of credit were permitted limited imports.

He stressed maize’s importance to poultry feed and said substituting rice made it difficult to achieve expected chicken and egg production levels. He also warned that possible El Niño conditions could threaten feed security and called for strategic maize reserves and a review of import restrictions.

His argument reinforces the need to treat maize as both a crop-income issue and a food-security input. But reliable reserve targets should be established through published demand and supply assessments rather than unsupported assumptions.

A policy framework for farmers and exporters

Reform does not require abandoning domestic maize growers or opening imports without safeguards. It requires five linked measures.

A more coherent maize policy should begin with a reliable national supply-and-demand assessment covering the requirements of broiler and layer production, dairy farming, Thriposha manufacturing and human consumption. Updated information on domestic harvests, available stocks and projected shortages would enable the Government to determine import quantities and timing based on actual market requirements rather than administrative discretion.

Such an approach should be supported by a predictable seasonal import mechanism that protects domestic maize growers during harvesting periods while allowing feed manufacturers to secure adequate supplies ahead of anticipated shortages. Greater transparency in import permit allocations, approved quantities and eligibility criteria would help minimise market distortions and prevent excessive concentration among importers.

However, protecting domestic maize farmers should not depend primarily on import restrictions and tariffs. Improving access to high-yielding seeds, irrigation, mechanised harvesting, drying and storage facilities, together with forward-purchasing agreements, would help increase productivity and reduce production costs. These interventions could strengthen farm incomes while gradually improving the competitiveness of locally produced maize without imposing additional costs on the poultry industry.

At the same time, the Government should consider a controlled raw material import mechanism for export-oriented poultry producers. Under such an arrangement, verified exporters could access maize and other essential feed ingredients at concessionary rates against documented production and export commitments. Appropriate monitoring, auditing and stock reconciliation would be necessary to prevent these imports from being diverted into the domestic market.

Beyond input costs, expanding poultry exports requires investment in animal disease surveillance, food safety certification, product traceability, modern processing facilities and refrigerated logistics. A coordinated public-private approach to these requirements would strengthen compliance with international market standards and improve Sri Lanka’s ability to compete in regional and global poultry markets. Ultimately, aligning agricultural protection with industrial competitiveness and export development should be the central objective of maize policy reform.

These reforms also demand coordination among agriculture, livestock, trade and fiscal authorities. Clear rules could be reviewed against practical indicators: domestic farm-gate prices, import approval times, feed costs, poultry output and export performance.

Decisions made to protect one commodity should be tested against their consequences for downstream production and export earnings. A published review would help distinguish genuine supply shortages from distribution problems and make policy adjustments more accountable.

Sri Lanka need not choose between protecting maize farmers and expanding poultry exports. The choice is between an unpredictable system of restrictions and a transparent policy that rewards domestic productivity while meeting genuine supply shortfalls.

If poultry is to become a stronger export earner, competitiveness must begin with the cost and reliability of its feed supply.

Under such a system, poultry processors producing for verified overseas markets could be permitted to import feed ingredients at concessionary rates, subject to strict documentation, audit requirements and controls against diversion into the domestic market.

This would help preserve domestic farmer protection while enabling exporters to compete on more commercially viable terms. Finally, export promotion must be supported by stronger industry infrastructure and international compliance.

Public-private investment in disease surveillance, food safety certification, modern processing facilities, traceability systems and refrigerated logistics will be necessary if Sri Lanka hopes to enter more demanding international markets. These measures should be coordinated through an integrated agricultural, industrial and trade development strategy rather than implemented through isolated policy interventions.

Protecting maize farmers and developing poultry exports are not mutually exclusive

Sri Lanka’s maize import policy should not be reduced to a choice between domestic farmer protection and unrestricted imports. Both agricultural livelihoods and livestock industry development are legitimate national priorities.

However, protecting maize farmers through unpredictable restrictions while expecting poultry producers to expand output, maintain affordable prices and compete in export markets creates an economically inconsistent policy environment. A more sustainable framework would combine targeted farmer support, productivity improvements, transparent import management and competitive access to essential feed ingredients.

Such an approach could strengthen domestic food security, improve poultry industry profitability, attract investment and create new opportunities for agricultural value-added exports. If Sri Lanka genuinely intends to move beyond import substitution and establish poultry as a significant export-oriented industry, competitiveness must be built across the entire production chain. That process begins not at the poultry processing plant or the export terminal, but with the availability, affordability and reliability of maize.

Protecting domestic maize farmers and expanding poultry exports need not be competing national objectives. Bridging the policy gap between them is ultimately a responsibility of the Government.

‘’The writer brings nearly 25 years of professional experience in journalism, media advocacy, public relations and reputation management, having worked with leading communications consultancies and industry associations across diverse sectors, including plantations, apparel, poultry, poverty reduction, health care and banking and finance. His expertise encompasses strategic communications, policy advocacy and stakeholder engagement, with a particular focus on economic and public policy issues. He is currently pursuing a Master’s degree in Economic and Public Policy Studies at the University of Colombo’’.

title: Personal Income Taxation - A growing burden for Sri Lankans and economy | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 20 October 2026 05:21
-     - 12

The Personal Income Taxation of Sri Lanka has adversely impacted the economy and affected the livelihood of the working-class and young professionals who are the backbone of our economy. 

Having the highest tax rate of 36% is not an issue, however all citizens should be entitled to have a reasonable tax-free income with sustainable tax rates and slabs. Taxing very low-income earners costs more in administrative collection efforts than it yields in actual revenue. 

In today’s context, when families are struggling to make ends meet, reducing the tax-free allowance to a mere Rs. 150,000 per month and increasing tax rates from 6% to 36% on small slabs is punitive. The taxes have resulted in a mass exodus of doctors, engineers, bankers, university professors, white collar and skilled workers. The exodus has affected major sectors, and businesses are forced to scale down their operations, because all of the emigrants’ process knowledge and business experience have departed with them too. 

Taxing people at source is an easy form of collecting taxes. It is most unjust to use this mandatory collection on those who are struggling to make a living when a large number of high-income individuals blatantly evade paying taxes either by not having tax files or by not declaring their full income. 

It is discriminatory that resident Sri Lankans have to pay tax on interest which goes up to 36%, whilst for non-resident Sri Lankans, the withholding tax rate of 10% is a final tax on the same Rupee deposit sources. It should be noted that wealthy Sri Lankan citizens have been advised by their tax advisors to transfer their Rupee deposits to closely connected persons who are or will take up non-resident status and pay tax at 10%, which is the final tax. The 10% Final Withholding Tax appears to be a form of tax avoidance granted to non-resident Sri Lankans. 

It would be more equitable and beneficial to fix the Withholding Tax rate on all Rupee deposit holders, both resident and non-resident Sri Lankans, at 15%, and make it a final tax, which would ensure certainty of tax revenue. This would also encourage the savings vital to increasing the country’s capital stock. It should be noted that funds deposited in banks/financial institutions are after paying the relevant taxation on earnings, and as such taxation on interest is double taxation. 

If every Sri Lankan pays his/her taxes, tax rates could come down in the future. Those responsible for tax policy should be independent and follow the four basic canons of taxation, which is Equity (citizens should pay taxes based on their ability to pay), Certainty (rules of taxation must be clear and predictable), Convenience (be collected at the most convenient time and in the most convenient manner for the taxpayer), and Economy (cost of collecting the tax should be as low as possible)

title: “Buddy-Racketeers” | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 20 October 2026 05:06
-     - 13

The image house of the Kotte Raja Maha Vihara is notable for its architectural and artistic features. It consists of two chambers, with the walls of the inner chamber adorned with Kandyan Era frescoes. The outer chamber appears to have been constructed more recently and features modern frescoes. The inner chamber has two entrances framed by sculpted Makara Thorana (Dragon arches). A unique feature is a framed portrait of Queen Victoria painted over the right-side entrance door, accompanied by two lions

The optics were as breathtaking as they were damning. On a Saturday, an opulent parade of luxury, chauffeured chariots rolled directly into the Kotte headquarters of the Kotte Sri Kalyani Samagri Dharma Maha Sangha Sabha of the Siam Nikaya.

 Out stepped saffron-clad potentates, oozing obesity and some limping with diabetic neuropathy, the telltale evidence of indolence masquerading as piety. 

 These Japanese, Korean, and German SUVs—capsules of wealth representing the absolute antithesis of Siddhartha’s doctrine of impermanence and renunciation—stood as symbols of the ultimate upward mobility of the Kotte Chapter›s prelates.

 These monks had not gathered to meditate on the deep crises of our economic recovery process or moral decay paralysing the nation. Instead, they convened an emergency conclave to defend a convicted, imprisoned colleague: Galagoda Aththe Gnanasara. 

 By forcefully demanding his immediate release and fiercely protesting the prison administration›s removal of his saffron robes under then existing regulations, these prelates sent an unmistakable, fearsomely toxic message to the citizenry: the robe is an absolute shield against the ordinary laws of this land.

 A watershed event in 1959

That shouldn’t surprise the Buddhists of this fortunate ‘Dharma-Deepa’. To borrow the razor-sharp pun coined by legendary journalist Tarzie Vittachi, these prelates have systematically operated as “Buddy-Racketeers.” 

The historical blueprint for this corporate monasticism was perfectly captured during the assassination of a Prime Minister, a watershed crisis we faced in 1959. 

Vittachi directed his biting double-entendre at Mapitigama Buddharakkhita, the then-powerful Chief Incumbent of the hallowed Kelaniya Raja Maha Vihara.

 The pun was a devastating indictment.  Buddharakkhita, whose name literally translated to “Protected by the Buddha,” had subverted his sacred vows to become a ruthless political kingmaker. He weaponised an influential network of political “buddies” to run highly lucrative commercial “rackets.” The irony was magnified by the sanctuary he controlled.

The Kelaniya Temple is   deeply revered by millions because chronicled tradition states it was consecrated by a personal visit by the Buddha himself. 

Operating a shadow corporate empire out of a temple of such mythic spiritual purity laid bare the utter rot eating into the post-independence state even to this day! 

Buddharakkhita’s fatal fallout with Prime Minister S. W. R. D. Bandaranaike was driven not by doctrinal disputes, but by a failed corporate undertaking. 

Having heavily financed and mobilised the monk-led campaign that swept Bandaranaike into power under the «Sinhala Only» wave of 1956, the «Buddy-Racketeer» expected immediate, untaxed financial dividends.

He was deeply aggrieved when the Prime Minister flatly refused to award a lucrative government monopoly to his venture, Colombo Shipping Lines, which aimed to corner state-subsidised rice imports from Burma and Thailand.

When Bandaranaike further blocked his plans for a state-licensed sugar enterprise, Buddharakkhita’s transition from a frustrated investor into a murderous conspirator was finalised.

The monk masterminded the Prime Minister›s assassination out of sheer spite. 

It set a terrifying precedent: when the democratic state refuses to bend to the financial greed of the robe, the robe will attempt to break the state.

Remarkably, despite being convicted by the Supreme Court and sentenced to life imprisonment, Buddharakkhita was never officially defrocked by his Nikaya, illustrating an early, absolute refusal by the monastic hierarchy to subject its own to secular criminal accountability.

An Ordained Nobility – A colonial legacy    

This resistance to state authority is rooted in a colonial legacy of institutionalised privilege. One needs only to visit the Kotte Raja Maha Vihara shrine room to see a stunning material manifestation of this alliance: a prominent portrait of Empress Victoria painted directly onto the temple walls. 

Far from a bizarre historical accident, it is the Siam Nikaya’s grateful, enduring acknowledgment of British imperial patronage.

Through the Buddhist Temporalities Ordinance, the British colonial administration effectively legalised and protected «monastic landlordism.»

By granting vast tracts of untaxed, state-secured land to specific temples and reinforcing elite caste-based hegemonies—such as the Radala-Goyigama dominance within the Malwatta and Asgiriya chapters—the colonial state transformed the Sangha into an untouchable class of landed aristocrats. 

Secularism and progressive governance have always been viewed by this monastic elite as existential threats to their inherited property, wealth, and systemic immunity.

As a result, whenever the state attempted to implement progressive legislation or equitable social reforms, the corporate Sangha has swiftly weaponised religious sentiment to torpedo them.

 In the mid-20th century, when progressive forces within various coalition governments attempted to introduce redistributive land reforms that would cap private holdings, the monastic landlord cartel fiercely opposed the legislation.

This systemic cancer reached its malignant zenith during the presidency of Mahinda Rajapaksa. The Rajapaksa regime fundamentally understood that its rampant institutional corruption, familial nepotism, and economic mismanagement could be shielded from public scrutiny if it systematically fed the beast of majoritarian paranoia. The final, tragic defense of this toxic paradigm is encapsulated by the political survival tactics of Ranil Wickremesinghe

They disingenuously framed property rights for wealthy temples as the defence of the ‘Buddha Sasana.’

More destructively, the Sangha has consistently served as the final burial ground for any rational, peaceful settlement of our historical ethnic discords. 

The historic Bandaranaike-Chelvanayakam Pact of 1957 and the Dudley-Chelvanayakam Pact of 1965—both offered modest, sensible frameworks for regional devolution and minority language rights.

These tentative accords were violently derailed by street protests orchestrated by monks who marched to the Colombo residences of prime ministers to demand their unconditional abrogation. 

Decades later, their unyielding hostility toward the 13th Amendment and any form of power-sharing continues to keep the country shackled to a suffocating, hyper-centralised state model that deliberately alienates its minority citizens.

The rise of the saffron cartel

These "Buddy Racketeers" have clearly failed to absorb or implement the profound thesis of Walpola Rahula Thero’s seminal 1946 work, Bhikshuvage Urumaya (The Heritage of the Bhikkhu). 

Rahula Thero argued that while the monk historically possessed a socio-political role, that role was strictly tied to selfless social service, intellectual enlightenment, and fighting for the freedom of the downtrodden. 

Instead, modern political monks have perverted this heritage. They have transformed it into a license for demagoguery, corporate enrichment, and chauvinistic extremism.

The upper echelons of the Sangha no longer serve as spiritual leaders. They are no longer trailblazers of the caliber of Hikkaduwe Sri Sumangala Thero, Welivitiye Soratha Thero, or the later sage Walpola Rahula Thero. 

Instead, they function as highly organised members of an economic and political cartel. This flagrant display of monastic arrogance is not a modern anomaly. It is not a sudden deviation from tradition.

Instead, it is the continuation of a long, dark history of political monasticism. For decades, these powerful forces—manipulated by crony elite classes and, in turn, manipulated by capricious monks who routinely outsmart their own patrons—have acted as a formidable barrier obstructing our slow, bitter crawl toward structural progress, secular governance, and true modernity.

This systemic cancer reached its malignant zenith during the presidency of Mahinda Rajapaksa. The Rajapaksa regime fundamentally understood that its rampant institutional corruption, familial nepotism, and economic mismanagement could be shielded from public scrutiny if it systematically fed the beast of majoritarian paranoia. 

The MR presidency aided by GR the soldier who never was a true warrior, deliberately cultivated and weaponised extremist monastic front groups, most notably the Bodu Bala Sena (BBS)—co-founded by none other than Galagoda Aththe Gnanasara.

Backed by State intelligence apparatuses and protected by political patronage, these extremist monks were given free rein to instigate anti-minority riots, vandalise property, and terrorise communities with complete impunity.

 By tethering its legitimacy to the absolute worst elements of the saffron cartel, the Rajapaksa presidency rapidly disintegrated into a viciously parochial, kleptocratic regime that bartered the country›s economic future for majoritarian cheers.

The cowardice of the secular elite

The final, tragic defence of this toxic paradigm is encapsulated by the political survival tactics of Ranil Wickremesinghe.

Long marketed to the international community as a sophisticated, Western-educated liberal and a champion of the rule of law, Wickremesinghe’s political calculus eventually exposed the sheer cowardice of the secular elite. 

His political alliance›s defence of Gnanasara—protesting the court-ordered return to prison, the removal of the monk’s robes and appeasing the Kotte prelates’ outrage—completes the vicious circle of state capitulation.

It proves that regardless of whether the regime in power is overtly nationalist or determinedly committed to make the republic inclusive, the secular state must either bow in terror before the saffron cartel or meet it head on. 

As long as our political classes continue to coddle these «Buddy-Racketeers,» allowing them to arrive in luxury chariots to dictate judicial outcomes and veto progressive state actions, the country will remain trapped in its post-independence malaise.

 True modernity and progress will remain a distant, impossible dream until the rule of law applies equally to all—whether one wears a civilian suit, a politician’s shawl, or the sacred robes of the Buddha.

title: War on rights: Protection from Organised Crimes Bill | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 20 October 2026 04:59
-     - 15

Progressive rhetoric but regressive actions 

The rhetoric of the National People’s Power (NPP) on the drug issue, prior to being elected, like their position on numerous issues, appeared progressive. It created hope that if elected they might adopt a health and human rights-based approach. After nearly two years in power, similar to their actions regarding other issues, the NPP Government is following in the footsteps of previous governments by enacting repressive laws that increase State power at the expense of the rights of citizens. 

Globally, the complex nature of drug use and drug dependence is often ignored when addressing drug trafficking, which has resulted in severe violations against persons who use drugs or have a drug dependency. These measures also restrict and undermine the rights of all citizens. Yet, the public mistakenly assume the law will only impact those who are connected to the drug trade. Hence, they, against their self-interest, usually support measures that undermine everyone’s human rights. 

The most recent addition to the basket of anti-human rights laws presented by the NPP Government is the Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill (POCB). Instead of addressing the root causes of drug trafficking and the violence associated with it, the proposed law will exacerbate the problem and lead to adverse consequences for several marginalised groups while enabling police impunity. 

Broad definitions: Building blocks of oppression

An organised criminal group (OCG) is defined in the UN Convention against Transnational Organised Crime (Palermo Convention), as ‘a structured group of three or more persons, existing for a period of time and acting in concert with the aim of committing one or more serious crimes or offences established in accordance with this Convention, in order to obtain, directly or indirectly, a financial or other material benefit’. The POCB uses the same definition in the interpretation (definition) section of the Bill, but section 4 of the Bill that describes the offence states that any person who acts with one or more person to commit a serious crime to obtain a material benefit will be liable to prosecution. The Bill also makes no mention of the need for the group to be structured as opposed to a random group of persons. It is pertinent to note the Palermo Convention’s definition has been critiqued for being broad, vague and failing to include adequate human rights safeguards. The outcome of this is demonstrated by the war on drugs’ disproportionate negative impact on marginalised communities, such as women, the poor and persons who have a drug dependence. 

According to the PCOB, the term ‘serious crime’ refers to offences which already exist in several Sri Lankan laws but become serious crimes when they are committed by a member of an organised criminal group. The purpose of the 72 page Bill is therefore not to create new offences but to increase the penalties for these offences along with the powers of the police, while lowering due process and fair trial safeguards to make prosecution and conviction easier. 

Under the PCOB a person can be deemed a member of an organised crime group based on broad, arbitrary, subjective factors. For instance, persons can be identified as gang members based on the style of dress, hand signs, language or tattoos if they correspond to those of an organised criminal group. Whether a person associates with members of an OCG or habitually visits places used by OCGs with knowledge the place is owned or occupied by an OCG are also criteria which can be used to determine a person’s membership of an OCG. These broad, arbitrary, sweeping identifying factors can be weaponised to label anyone a gang member. A person can also be identified by other members as a member of an organised criminal group. However, being identified by other members alone should not be accepted as adequate evidence of membership; passive membership without active participation in the group’s criminal activities is not an offence in many jurisdictions. In countries such as El Salvador, where people report persons they suspect of gang association with no evidence, the informant culture has led to mass arbitrary detention and wrongful prosecution.

According to the PCOB, the term ‘serious crime’ refers to offences which already exist in several Sri Lankan laws but become serious crimes when they are committed by a member of an organised criminal group. The purpose of the 72 page Bill is therefore not to create new offences but to increase the penalties for these offences along with the powers of the police, while lowering due process and fair trial safeguards to make prosecution and conviction easier

The offences listed as serious crime if done by a member of an OCG include offences under the Excise Ordinance, advertising unlawful gambling, infringement of copyright, patents and marks, harbouring a military deserter, obstructing a public servant in the discharge of their public duties and exploring for mines without a license. Just as the PSTB elevates a broad range of offences to terrorism, the PCOB elevates a broad range of offences to organised crime. 

In practice, this law can be used to target persons with drug dependence, a serious health issue. For example, if three young persons who are dependent on drugs but do not have money to purchase drugs meet with a member of an OCG to obtain drugs, they may be forced by the dealer to undertake tasks for him in lieu of payment. They may do this often and hence would visit places frequented by the OCG and obtain a material benefit, i.e. drugs. They might hence be prosecuted for engaging in a serious crime in concert with members of an OCG instead of being treated as persons with a substance use disorder and provided treatment and assistance to deal with drug dependence and its physical and psychological effects. 

Freedom of expression and right to privacy

The Bill prohibits making the name of a victim of a serious crime public but allows the Officer-in-Charge of a police station or the police officer undertaking the investigation to make it public in good faith for the purposes of investigation. The Bill does not require the police to obtain the consent of the victim to do so. This instrumentalises the victim for investigatory purposes, violates the victim’s privacy and denies them agency to decide whether or not to go public. 

The PCOB prohibits reporting court proceedings concerning an offence under this Act without the approval of the court, which effectively makes trials under this law secret trials. It undermines media freedom and prevents highlighting any due process issues and shortcomings in the trial process and thereby lessens the accountability of the State. 

Entrenching impunity of State entities

Militarisation of law enforcement which has been included in the Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill (PSTB) is replicated in the POCB with the police empowered to obtain the assistance of the military to conduct an arrest. The rank of the police officer who has the power to make such a request, nor the criteria/reasons for requesting assistance have been stipulated. This can lead to broken or even non-existent chains of command: turning the current culture of impunity into a legalised state of impunity. 

After arrest the person must be produced before the Magistrate within 72 hours but the Bill says if the arrest is made “within Sri Lanka’ the travel time shall be excluded when calculating the 72 hours. Since there are over 70 Magistrates courts in Sri Lanka, excluding travel time from the 72 hours within which a person is produced before a magistrate cannot be justified. 

The sections on detention in the POCB have been cut and pasted from the PSTB. For example, a detention order (DO) is issued for 2 months and the Magistrate has no option but to give effect to it. Where there is no DO the Magistrate has to remand the person. Detention is hence the default outcome. The Secretary to the Ministry of Defence (MOD) issues the DO upon request of Inspector General of Police (IGP) or the Deputy Inspector General (DIG) and the maximum period of detention is one year. 

To extend the DO, the police via the Attorney-General (AG) must request an extension from the High Court (HC). If the HC refuses to extend the DO, the HC must remand or release the person on bail. In this instance too the judge has no power to discharge the person, i.e. release the person from the case. The pattern of undermining the authority of the judiciary, which seems to be based on the premise the executive/police know what’s best, is observable in several draft laws presented by the Government. 

Like in PSTB, the POCB says the police officer shall take any measure as appropriate to prevent a crime under this law. Such broad powers can embolden an already power drunk police force to commit violations with impunity. The Bill allows police to send evidence directly to Government Analyst instead of via court; this removes judicial oversight to ensure the chain of custody is not broken and reduce the possibility of evidence tampering. 

The powers of the police are enhanced by empowering the DIG to obtain information from any telecom or data service provider without a court order to determine the identity of the caller, calls or the tower location of a device. The police must only inform the Magistrate in writing, which is a gateway to obtaining a broad remit of information and can pave the way for abuses. The information technology aspect of POCB has been discussed extensively by Dr Sanjana Hattotuwa. 

Restriction of liberty: the default 

A person who is not detained under a DO and is instead remanded immediately may be released on bail. However, the Bill is silent on whether bail can be granted to a person initially detained under a DO. Hence, the assumption is there is no bail for those who are initially detained under a DO. This discrimination/distinction cannot be justified. 

The Bill states a person shall not be held in remand for more than a year and if the indictment is not filed within a year they can be released on bail. Just as in the PSTB, this indicates that a person who is indicted cannot be released on bail until they are acquitted. Therefore, a person who is detained under a DO can be detained for a year then remanded for a year and if indicted within a year then remanded until the conclusion of the trial. In such a scenario if the person is acquitted then the person would have been in detention for many years. 

Similar to the POCB, the PSTB allows the Magistrate to issue restriction orders with no maximum time limit stipulated for the lifetime of such orders, which means it can be in place for years. 

Attack on due process rights: Reintroducing police confession

The admissibility of confessions made to a police officer of the rank of ASP and above, which has been removed from the PSTB has been included in the POCB despite the long history of this provision, which remains in the Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA), being used by the police to extract confessions under torture. This provision normalised torture as a method of interrogation and the POCB will entrench it further. The burden of proof is reversed and instead of the State having to prove the case against the person, the person must prove the statement was obtained under duress. The PCOB allows the confession to be used against another person as well if it is corroborated by other evidence- can even be circumstantial evidence- to convict a person of a serious crime.

Under the PCOB a person can be deemed a member of an organised crime group based on broad, arbitrary, subjective factors. For instance, persons can be identified as gang members based on the style of dress, hand signs, language or tattoos if they correspond to those of an organised criminal group. Whether a person associates with members of an OCG or habitually visits places used by OCGs with knowledge the place is owned or occupied by an OCG are also criteria which can be used to determine a person’s membership of an OCG. These broad, arbitrary, sweeping identifying factors can be weaponised to label anyone a gang member

Although the PCOB requires the statement to be video recorded and the person making the confession to obtain advice from a lawyer prior to making the confession, if a person is tortured or subject to threat prior to the statement being recorded these safeguards will not protect them. 

The Bill allows the judge to alter the indictment at any time during trial if the court is of the opinion that the person is not a member of an organised crime group and did not act to further a common criminal objective. Moreover, if a confession has been entered as evidence in the case, the PCOB states it should be excluded and the offence should be tried under other law. There is no justifiable rationale for allowing a police confession to be used if the person is a member of an organised crime group and not if the person is not a member. This demonstrates human rights protections against torture and fair trial standards have been lowered for persons accused of being a member of an OCG, i.e.  if a person is accused of being a member of an OCG then the person can be tortured and a (most likely false) confession obtained to ensure a conviction. If a person contradicts a statement they made, they can be tried for giving false evidence which can be done easily because the Bill says the State only must prove the contradiction between the two statements and does not have to demonstrate which statement is false. These provisions show the aim is to prevent accused persons from challenging confessions given under duress for fear they may be penalised further. The Bill stipulates certain protective measures to be taken when a person makes a statement to the Magistrate but does not require the same protections to be applied when the statement is made to the police officer. The POCB hence deprives a person of protection when they are in the most vulnerable state.
